cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-47-christ.summary: Across a valley from the psalmist rises the 'city of our God' on its holy mountain, and in the portico of its temple stands the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos holding a globe, with people coming out on either side: 'God is known in her palaces'. Daughters of Judah dance around the hill and talk in the towers. It is one of the drawing's most charming architectural fantasies.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
Its text is written in rustic capitals, an archaic script that once led scholars to date the manuscript to the 6th century; the drawings are now recognised as Carolingian.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-47-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:monumental-san-road-to-emmaus.summary: The risen Christ, bearded and haloed, walks between two disciples on the road to Emmaus, the walled town visible on a hill at the upper left. He turns to speak with them as they travel, unrecognised until the breaking of bread.
facts: On the south wall the thirteen Passion and Resurrection scenes show Christ bearded; the cycle omits both the Flagellation and the Crucifixion.
The scenes were not arranged in biblical order but are thought to follow the Gospel readings of the Lenten liturgy in Theodoric's palace church.

cur:monumental2-abdallah-nirqi-nativity.summary: The Virgin, wrapped in a dark brown mantle, reclines diagonally on a great patterned mattress strewn with rosettes, beside a gridded structure representing the manger and stable in which the swaddled Child lay; at the left the shepherds and other small figures approach, one in a yellow robe. The painting is badly abraded, and the Child himself is now barely legible within the manger.
facts: Abdallah Nirqi was one of the Lower Nubian sites investigated during the UNESCO campaign of the 1960s before its flooding by Lake Nasser.
cur:monumental2-abdallah-nirqi-nativity.notes: Facts follow the Commons description (Nativity, church of Abdallah Nirqi, 10th century, Coptic Museum, Cairo); not confirmed against a museum record. The Christ Child is very faint in the photograph.
